summary: The agent implemented and locally validated direct Map-to-iterable and iterable-to-Map entry mappings, but the hidden suite exposed a missing integration path for automatically forged mappings between Map and iterable bean properties. Baseline tests all passed; only 2 of 32 new tests passed because the shared ScheduleBookMapper fixture failed compilation.
quick_failure_summary: Automatic Map-to-List and List-to-Map mappings for bean properties are not forged, so the hidden mapper fixture fails compilation.

details.reasoning: The implementation reclassified direct cross-container methods through SourceMethod and extended IterableMappingMethod, but it did not update PropertyMapping to forge Map-to-iterable and iterable-to-Map conversions when those container types occur as bean properties. Consequently, ScheduleBookMapper cannot map Map<String, Schedule> schedules to List<FlattenedSchedule> schedules or reverse it, and compilation reports that the List return type is abstract plus missing property mapping methods. The reference solution explicitly adds these branches in PropertyMapping and uses a dedicated IterableToMapMappingMethod builder.
details.secondary_factors: The agent's added tests exercised direct mapping methods only, so they did not cover the missing bean-property integration. The hidden test class compiles many fixtures together, causing this one compilation defect to fan out into 30 failed test invocations; that amplifies the count but does not invalidate the underlying failure.

justification.issue_description: Missing automatic forging of Map-to-iterable and iterable-to-Map element mappings for bean properties.
justification.evidence: The prompt broadly requires support for mapping a Map<K,V> to an iterable or array result and the reverse, with normal mapping-method selection; it does not limit support to top-level mapper signatures. In the visible codebase, PropertyMapping.forge already contains dedicated branches for collection/array-to-iterable and Map-to-Map mappings, showing that container mapping features must also be forged for bean properties. Existing collection tests and models exercise forged collection and map property mappings. The agent inspected MapperCreationProcessor and direct container builders but did not add the corresponding PropertyMapping branches present in the reference solution.
justification.verdict_reasoning: This is a missed requirement rather than an undocumented edge case or arbitrary hidden-test mismatch. A competent MapStruct developer should expect a new container mapping family to participate in automatic property mapping, and the visible PropertyMapping architecture makes that integration point reasonably inferable. The agent completed substantial working code, so this is not early termination; the dominant defect is the omitted property-forging path.

problem_assessment.notes: The task is broad and requires coordinated changes across method classification, model generation, templates, entry construction, type bounds, and property forging, but the reference solution demonstrates it is solvable. The hidden suite is deterministic and covers the stated behaviors. Its shared compilation fixture makes one compile failure appear as 30 failures, which reduces diagnostic granularity but does not make the test broken or unfair.

evidence: JUnit reports 3,641 baseline tests with zero failures or errors, and the verifier reports baseline_passed=True.
The new-suite failures are deterministic Java compilation diagnostics in ScheduleBookMapper for unsupported Map/List property conversion, directly tied to the missing implementation path.
The trajectory shows the agent's focused tests and Maven verify/checkstyle validation completed successfully, so the toolchain was functional.
The only observed tool hiccups were a missing rg executable and one closed write_stdin session; the agent immediately switched to find/grep or reran the command and was not materially diverted.
environment_assessment.finding: No meaningful external environment or verifier blocker was found; the failure is explained by a missing integration path in the implementation.
